metadata.note: Dr. Dorsey Syng Baker's Walla Walla and Columbia River Railroad, the 'Rawhide Railroad' -- the first railroad in the Pacific Northwest other than the short portage lines around the Columbia rapids, and the reason Walla Walla was for a time the largest town in Washington Territory. Incorporated at Walla Walla in 1868, surveyed 1871 by Gen. James Tilton, graded from 1872 under Major Sewell Truax, opened ten miles east of Wallula in 1873, reached Whitman Station (Frenchtown, now Lowden) in 1874, and was completed into Walla Walla on October 23 1875: about 32 miles of 3-ft narrow gauge, built cheaply with strap iron nailed to wooden stringers. Its purpose was to get Walla Walla Valley wheat down to the Columbia River steamboat landing at Wallula without wagon freight. Ainsworth's Oregon Railway and Navigation Company negotiated the purchase through 1878-1879 and was operating the road under its own name by March 31 1880; Villard's OR&N standard-gauged it in 1881 to connect with the Northern Pacific building east from Portland (see northern_pacific.geojson). The WW&CR corporate name survived until it was consolidated into the OR&N in 1910, which is where these features end -- the corridor itself is still in service today as the short-line Blue Mountain Railroad. Four features cover the construction stages and the two operating eras; a fifth is the Blue Mountain branch.

geometry_sources: Wallula - Walla Walla main line: real-traced from OpenStreetMap (Overpass), shortest rail path over the surviving alignment, now the Blue Mountain Railroad / UP branch. 626 points, 52.84 km / 32.84 mi -- which matches the ~32-mile figure in the sources, so the modern track is taken to follow Baker's route closely.

The 1873 and 1874 construction-stage features are the same traced line truncated at 9.99 mi (the 'ten miles east of Wallula' opened in 1873) and at 19.79 mi (the point nearest Lowden, i.e. Whitman Station / Frenchtown).

Blue Mountain branch: APPROXIMATE. The Whitman-Milton portion was abandoned in 1883 and nothing of it survives in OpenStreetMap, so this is a seven-point waypoint sketch from Whitman Station southeast down the valley toward Dry Creek, ending southwest of Milton-Freewater. It draws 11.6 mi against the documented 14 mi, so the real alignment was more circuitous than shown; treat the shape as indicative only.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Timetable frequencies for every era -- the daily-mixed-train headways here are estimates, not documented schedules. Also unsourced: running times (the ~11 mph narrow-gauge figure is from general accounts, not a timetable), the exact Walla Walla depot location and the precise east end of the original 1875 track, the exact location of Whitman Station beyond 'Old Highway 12 and Frenchtown Road', the exact site of Blue Mountain Station, and whether the 1873 railhead ended exactly where the 10-mile point falls on the modern alignment. One source (a Whitman Wire piece) describes the branch as running 19 miles southeast from Whitman rather than 14 miles south; the 14-mile figure is used here because two sources agree on it. Note also that the features here end in 1910 with the WW&CR's consolidation into the OR&N, so the Walla Walla end of the Walla Walla-Wallula-Riparia-Lewiston chain disappears from the map after 1910 even though the track remained in service; no OWR&N-era successor feature for the Walla Walla branch has been researched or drawn. The ICC valuation for the WW&CR describes its branch as running 'from Barrett to Blue Mountain, Oreg.' and dates construction 1874-1879 with standard-gauging 1881-1883, where the sources used here name the junction Whitman Station; whether Barrett is a later name for the same point has not been confirmed.
metadata.lewiston_connection: The WW&CR never approached Lewiston, Idaho, and no through PASSENGER service ever linked Walla Walla with Lewiston. Walla Walla and Lewiston became physically connected only on July 7 1908, when the Oregon, Washington and Idaho Railroad opened Riparia-Lewiston (owi_riparia_lewiston.geojson), reachable from Wallula over the Snake River cutoff of 1899 (snake_river_valley_wallula_riparia.geojson) -- both now drawn, so the physical chain Walla Walla-Wallula-Riparia-Lewiston is visible on this map for 1908-1910. But that cutoff was built in 1899 expressly to provide 'a better route to Spokane than the existing line via Walla Walla', i.e. it bypassed Walla Walla nine years before Lewiston was connected at all. Walla Walla appears nowhere in the Camas Prairie passenger schedules: the July 1954 through Portland-Lewiston sleeper was switched at Ayer, and Camas Prairie trains 73/74 ran Ayer-Lewiston. A Walla Walla passenger for Lewiston had to change trains.

segments.note: Dr. Dorsey Syng Baker's line, built east from the Columbia River steamboat landing at Wallula. Grading began in 1872 under Major Sewell Truax (Baker had hired Gen. James Tilton to survey the 32-mile route in 1871); the first ten miles opened for traffic in 1873. Rails were wooden stringers with strap iron nailed on top, which gave the road its nicknames -- the Rawhide Railroad and the Strap Iron Railroad -- rawhide being wrapped around rails after 'snakehead' failures. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Completed into Walla Walla on October 23 1875 -- the first railroad in the Pacific Northwest other than the short portage lines around the Columbia rapids. About 32 miles, 3-ft narrow gauge. It broke the wagon-freight monopoly on hauling Walla Walla Valley wheat down to the Columbia River steamboats at Wallula, and Baker was accused of gouging on rates in return. Purchase negotiations with Capt. John Ainsworth and the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company ran through 1878-1879; OR&N was operating the whole property under its own name by March 31 1880. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: A 14-mile narrow-gauge branch off the Walla Walla and Columbia River at Whitman Station, begun by the Oregon Steam Navigation Company in spring 1878 toward Weston, Oregon. It never got there: it opened as far as Blue Mountain Station, southwest of present-day Milton-Freewater along Dry Creek, on September 15 1879. It was left narrow gauge when the parent line was standard-gauged in 1881 because part of it was meant to be absorbed into a longer route; in spring 1883 the ten miles from Milton to Blue Mountain were regauged as part of the Walla Walla-Pendleton line and the Whitman-Milton stretch was abandoned. This branch is what makes up the 46 miles of track usually quoted for the WW&CR. ALIGNMENT IS APPROXIMATE -- see metadata. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
